title: Java: when do you actually need `new`?
description:
A question that trips up every Java beginner: when do you have to write the word `new`, and when can you skip it? This Short uses the `Counter` class from the Java Mastery Path methods lesson to show the split. Instance methods like `increment()` and `getCount()` act on one object's data, so they need a `Counter` built with `new`. A `static` method like `Counter.describe()` belongs to the class itself and needs no object at all.

Source lesson(s):
- https://sigilipelli.github.io/java-mastery-path/level-1/04-methods-parameters/

#Shorts

beats.narration: Here's a question that trips up every Java beginner. When do you have to write the word new, and when can you skip it entirely?
Look at this Counter class. The count field, plus increment and getCount, are instance methods. They work on one specific object's data.
So there are two kinds. A static method belongs to the class itself. An instance method needs a real object to act on.
You build a Counter with new, call increment twice, and getCount returns two. But describe is static, so Counter dot describe needs no object at all.
That's the whole rule. Instance data needs new. Class level behavior doesn't. Once you see it, you'll never guess again.
